strengths: Novel core insight: Using the semantically empty initial token as a universal, task-agnostic control point is clever and contrasts effectively with prior attention-tuning methods requiring task-specific token identification
Strong theoretical foundation with clear mathematical formalization (Equations 3-6) showing how attention scaling preserves relative proportions while modulating differences across tokens

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 15 datasets across 3 task categories, 4 LLMs with different attention implementations, extensive robustness checks covering resource constraints, context length, few-shot learning, quantization, and prompt variations

Thorough analytical investigation: Layer-wise analysis reveals consistent trends with earlier layers more impactful; head-level analysis identifies heterogeneous responses (up-effective vs down-effective heads)
Substantial improvements on text classification tasks (11.71% for Llama-3.1-8B) with consistent gains across multiple models and implementations

Practical applicability with minimal computational overhead, works across different attention implementations (Eager, SDPA, Flash), and can be adapted for cases where direct attention modification is infeasible
weaknesses: Misleading 'training-free' claim: Method requires 500-sample validation set with ground-truth labels for head profiling. This is parameter-training-free but validation-data dependent, undermining a key claimed advantage. Limitation acknowledged only in Appendix I

Insufficient mechanistic understanding: Paper lacks clear explanation for WHY modifying initial token attention helps universally across diverse tasks. Explanations (flattening for SST-2, sharpening for BoolQ) feel post-hoc rather than predictive

Highly task-dependent effectiveness undermines universality claims: Classification +11.71% (substantial), QA tasks +2.64% (modest), MT-Bench conversation +0.162 points (marginal, likely within noise). Practical utility unclear for practitioners

Validation set overfitting: Head classification is task-specific and performed on a fixed validation set without cross-validation or robustness checks. No analysis of whether head labels transfer across different validation sets or tasks

Weak theoretical explanation for head heterogeneity: Speculation about functional roles (Section 2.4) lacks empirical evidence. Why certain heads prefer increased vs decreased attention to an 'empty' token remains unexplained
Limited baseline comparisons: Only compares with ACT and AutoPASTA; ACT cannot be evaluated on 2/4 models. Missing comparisons with other inference-time adaptations and simpler alternatives
Lack of statistical rigor: No error bars, confidence intervals, significance tests, or variance reporting across seeds. MT-Bench improvements may not exceed noise margins

Arbitrary methodological choices: 'Top 40% of heads' percentage appears arbitrary (Figure 8 shows sensitivity). 'Dominant head type' selection rule is vague. Different head percentages yield substantially different results
Marginal practical improvements for 2 of 3 task categories: QA (+2.64%) and conversation (+0.162 points) improvements are small, raising questions about practical significance and generalizability
Limited architectural diversity: Only tested on Llama, Qwen, and DeepSeek families. Unclear if findings generalize to significantly different model architectures or non-decoder-only models

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 4 models and 15 datasets with systematic analysis of layer-wise and head-wise effects
Clear mathematical formalization in Section 2.1 showing how initial token attention scaling compresses/expands differences among subsequent tokens
Extensive robustness studies (Appendices B-H) demonstrating effectiveness under quantization, context length variations, few-shot settings, and prompt variations
Well-structured ablations investigating the effect of different head proportions, scaling matrices (attention vs. key states), and resource constraints
Clear presentation with effective visualizations (Figures 2-5) that make the empirical findings accessible
weaknesses: Misleading 'training-free' and 'task-agnostic' framing: Method requires labeled validation data for head classification and scaling factor selection (buried in Section 2.6, contradicted in Appendix I Limitations)

Limited novelty: Core contribution is applying existing attention scaling to a different token; initial tokens as attention sinks and token-level attention tuning already well-established in prior work

Inconsistent and modest improvements: 11.71% on classification but only 2.64% on QA tasks and 0.162 points on MT-Bench (9-point scale); AutoPASTA achieves 60.18 vs ZeroTuning's 61.48 on multiple-choice (1.3 point margin)
No statistical significance testing: No confidence intervals, error bars, or hypothesis tests provided; single random seed (42) reported; improvements of 1-3% require statistical validation
Incomplete theoretical understanding: Paper speculates that heads 'specialize' but provides no mechanistic evidence; explanations for why sharpening/flattening helps are intuitive but unvalidated

Unfair baseline comparison: AutoPASTA not fairly analyzed for computational cost or validation set requirements; ACT comparison incomplete across models; advantages over AutoPASTA marginal on multiple-choice tasks
Validation set requirement not transparent: 500-sample validation set needed for head profiling, but no analysis of sensitivity to validation set size or practical availability

Limited evaluation scope: Only instruction-tuned models tested; unclear if method works on base models; task selection may favor domains where method is effective; no evaluation on complex reasoning or generation tasks
MT-Bench results undermine practical impact: 0.162-0.266 point improvements on 9-point scale are marginally above noise; insufficient motivation for practitioners to adopt
Missing key analyses: No error propagation analysis, no cross-task transferability of head classifications, no discussion of computational overhead relative to baselines

strengths: Novel and well-motivated insight that the semantically empty initial token serves as a universal, task-agnostic control point for steering model behavior, avoiding biases of task-specific token selection

Solid theoretical foundation with clear mathematical analysis (Equations 3-6) explaining how initial token attention scaling redistributes attention while preserving relative proportions among other tokens
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 4 models with different attention implementations, 15 datasets, 3 task categories, with extensive ablations and robustness checks in appendices

Excellent mechanistic understanding through layered analysis: consistent superiority of initial token tuning (Section 2.2), clear layer-wise patterns (Section 2.3), and discovery of heterogeneous attention head behaviors (Sections 2.4-2.5)
Strong and consistent empirical results: 11.71% average improvement on classification (up to 22% on SUBJ), 2.64% on QA, 0.162 on MT-Bench, consistently outperforming AutoPASTA and ACT baselines

Demonstrated robustness across diverse settings: works under resource constraints, long contexts, few-shot learning, different quantization levels, decoding strategies, and prompt variations (Appendices B-H)
Practical implementation that adapts to different attention implementations (eager, SDPA, Flash) by tuning key/query states when direct attention modification is infeasible
Clear and well-organized presentation with excellent visualizations and intuitive explanations of the core contribution
weaknesses: Claims of 'training-free' and 'supervision-free' are overstated: method requires labeled validation set (500 samples) for head profiling and scaling factor determination, undermining the unsupervised framing despite being parameter-efficient

Limited theoretical justification for WHY the method works: explains HOW attention is redistributed but lacks deep mechanistic understanding of task-specific benefits; explanations for SST-2 vs BoolQ are post-hoc and superficial

Varying effectiveness across task types (11.71% for classification vs 2.64% for QA) without adequate analysis of why or guidance on when to expect larger gains, suggesting task-dependent applicability

Baseline comparisons are limited: ACT cannot be evaluated on models other than Llama-3.1-8B due to attention map requirements; gap vs AutoPASTA on QA (1.3%) is much smaller than on classification (7.7%)

Head selection mechanism lacks principled guidance: categorization of up/down-effective heads is entirely task-dependent with high variability (Figure 4), requiring validation-set evaluation to select optimal 40-70% of heads
Limited evaluation on complex reasoning tasks: no assessment on longer-context generation, chain-of-thought reasoning, or multi-step planning; MT-Bench improvements are modest (0.162-0.266 points)
Absence of failure mode analysis: results appear uniformly positive without discussing tasks where ZeroTuning hurts performance or models where it's less effective
Generalization scope limited to decoder-only transformers (Llama, Qwen, DeepSeek); unclear if findings transfer to encoder-decoder models, vision transformers, or other architectures
Incremental novelty relative to prior token-level attention tuning work (PASTA, AutoPASTA, ACT); main contribution is focusing on initial token rather than task-specific tokens
Missing statistical rigor: single validation set per experiment with fixed seed; no confidence intervals or multiple runs reported to assess variance in results

strengths: Strong empirical results: Consistent improvements across 15 datasets and 4 models (e.g., +19.9% classification, +4.5% QA) outperforming more complex baselines
Elegant simplicity: Training-free method requiring only ~4 lines of code modification, works with quantized inference and multiple attention implementations (SDPA, FlashAttention)
Solid theoretical foundation: Clear mathematical formalization (Section 3.1) with rigorous proof of monotonic control over attention distributions via scaling factor γ
Comprehensive experimental analysis: Systematic investigation across layers, heads, context lengths, few-shot scenarios, quantization levels, and prompt variations
Practical applicability: Both supervised and unsupervised variants provided; kernel-agnostic design with fallback to key state scaling for optimized kernels
Honest limitation discussion: Clear delineation in Appendix D of when method works (uncertain errors) vs. fails (high-confidence mistakes); positioned as complementary to fine-tuning
Robust performance: Maintains gains across diverse conditions including quantization (4-bit, 8-bit), extended contexts, few-shot settings, and prompt variations
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: Core contribution builds on well-established attention sink phenomenon (Xiao et al. 2023, Barbero et al. 2025); main insight is leveraging known property rather than discovering new principle

Insufficient mechanistic understanding: Why the method works remains unclear—entropy correlation observed but not explained; head heterogeneity (up/down-effective) empirically documented but causally unexplained; task-specific γ preferences only post-hoc analyzed

Experimental rigor concerns: (1) Validation set leakage—supervised variant calibrates hyperparameters on fixed val set potentially biasing test comparison; (2) No statistical significance testing, error bars, or confidence intervals despite some modest improvements; (3) Greedy decoding as primary setting limits scope

Unsupervised variant limitations: Requires test set search for γ risking overfitting; Appendix E.1 reveals unreliable entropy landscape with format/bias traps and competing peaks; underperforms supervised (~0.5 point gap); complex failure modes not adequately addressed

Generalization questions: (1) Scope limited to decoder-only instruction-tuned models; unclear generalization to base models, encoder-decoder, or VLMs; (2) 'Task-agnostic' claim overstated—requires task-specific γ tuning; (3) Unclear scaling to very large models (tested max 14B)

Modest theoretical depth: Proposition 1's monotonicity result is straightforward calculus; lacks optimal γ analysis, convergence properties, or mechanistic explanation of why initial token tuning specifically helps

Head analysis lacks depth: Binary up/down-effective classification seems oversimplified; UP+DOWN hybrid underperforms suggesting complex interactions poorly understood; no analysis of functional roles these heads play
Limited baseline comparison: Only ACT and AutoPASTA compared; temperature scaling dismissed in appendix rather than rigorously evaluated; missing other recent inference-time optimization methods
MT-Bench dialogue improvements very small (+0.162): Suggests method effectiveness varies by task type; limited to classification-like tasks
Missing ablations: Effect of scaling different special tokens unclear; interaction with in-context examples underexplored; validation set construction details incomplete

strengths: Elegant simplicity: The method requires only 4 lines of code modifications and works across different attention implementations (FlashAttention, SDPA).
Comprehensive empirical analysis: Systematic investigation of layer-wise and head-wise effects with well-designed decomposition experiments (Sections 3.2-3.5).
Broad experimental validation: 15 datasets across 3 task categories with 4 models showing consistent improvements (19.9% on classification, 4.5% on QA).
Extensive robustness evaluation: Well-documented performance under varied conditions (long contexts, quantization, few-shot, prompt variations) with extensive appendices.
Methodological integrity: Honest discussion of limitations (Appendix D) clearly delineating what the method can and cannot do (unlocking latent knowledge vs. correcting confident errors).
Practical variants: Both supervised and unsupervised modes with clear trade-offs, addressing label scarcity scenarios.
weaknesses: Limited novelty of core contribution: Initial token as 'attention sink' is well-documented (Xiao et al. 2023, Barbero et al. 2025); the contribution reduces to simple scaling (Eq. 2-4), which is incremental relative to existing attention tuning methods.

Shallow theoretical insight: Proposition 1 (monotonic relationship) is straightforward calculus; the analysis describes HOW the distribution changes but NOT WHY scaling helps performance across diverse tasks or when/why the approach should succeed or fail.

Experimental setup concerns: (1) Supervised variant uses 500-sample validation set calibration that may give unfair advantage vs. baselines; (2) ACT only evaluated on one model due to attention map requirements, severely limiting baseline comparisons; (3) No comparison with temperature scaling despite claiming different mechanisms; (4) 60+ comparisons without multiple testing correction; (5) No error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

Unsupervised variant reliability issues: Appendix E.1 reveals significant problems where entropy minima correspond to wrong answers (format trap, bias amplification trap); method works only by averaging across datasets, limiting generalization to new distributions.

Head-specific tuning underdeveloped: Explanation for heterogeneity is speculative; UP+DOWN strategy underperforms, suggesting binary categorization is incomplete; lacks theoretical justification for why heads should specialize this way.

Generalization gaps: All experiments use instruction-tuned models (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Llama-2-13B-Chat, Qwen-2-7B, DeepSeek-R1-14B); no evaluation on base models, smaller LLMs, other architectures (GPT, T5, encoder-decoder), or novel domains; applicability across architectures remains uncertain.

Misleading claims: Paper claims 'no task-specific token identification' but supervised mode requires validation set calibration; 'ZeroTuning' name suggests no tuning but both variants involve calibration; entropy minimization is not fully unsupervised.

Missing key comparisons: No empirical comparison with temperature scaling (only theoretical argument in Appendix D); incomplete ablations on validation set size sensitivity; missing transfer studies across tasks.

strengths: Elegant simplicity and strong practical applicability: Only 4 lines of code modification, kernel-agnostic (SDPA, FlashAttention), and compatible with quantization, making it immediately deployable
Sound theoretical framework: Rigorous mathematical formalization (Eqs. 2-6) and Proposition 1 proving monotonic relationship between initial token attention and tuning effect magnitude
Comprehensive systematic investigation: Multi-dimensional analysis across token positions, layers, and attention heads with clear evidence that initial token outperforms other positions
Broad experimental validation: 4 LLM architectures, 15 datasets across 3 task categories, consistent improvements (19.9% classification, 4.5% QA), outperforming complex baselines (Auto-PASTA, ACT)
Extensive robustness testing: Thorough evaluation under long contexts (300+ tokens), quantization (4-8 bit), few-shot learning (1-2 shot), prompt variations, and multiple decoding strategies

Valuable insights about attention mechanisms: Discovery of inverse entropy-accuracy correlation enabling unsupervised variant; identification of up-effective vs down-effective heads; different task-type preferences
Honest assessment of limitations: Clear characterization of when method succeeds (uncertain errors) vs fails (high-confidence errors); transparent discussion of extreme tuning failure modes
Excellent presentation and completeness: Well-organized writing, clear visualizations, comprehensive appendices with detailed error analysis and mechanistic examples
weaknesses: Limited core novelty: Initial token as attention sink is well-established (Xiao et al. 2023, Barbero et al. 2025); contribution is primarily recognizing existing phenomenon as tuning lever rather than discovering new mechanism

Incomplete mechanistic understanding: Why is initial token optimal compared to other positions? Why do heads show heterogeneous responses (up-effective vs down-effective)? Why should entropy minimization improve task accuracy? These lack rigorous theoretical justification
Task-dependent effectiveness: 19.9% improvement on classification but only 4.5% on QA and 0.16 points on dialogue (MT-Bench); method works substantially better for some tasks than others

Calibration requirements and generalization concerns: Supervised variant requires validation data (500 samples); unsupervised variant is 0.5 points less effective; evaluation limited to instruction-tuned models with no analysis of base model performance

Unsupervised variant limitations: Section E.1 reveals concerning failure modes (format trap, bias amplification trap) where entropy minimization is unreliable at individual sample level; real-world applicability in label-scarce scenarios unclear

Incomplete baseline comparisons: ACT evaluated only on Llama-3.1-8B; multiple '—' entries in Tables 1-2; no comparison with other inference-time methods (temperature scaling, layer-wise adaptation); cannot fully assess relative performance

Missing statistical rigor: No error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests; some improvements are modest (2-4% on QA); variance across runs not reported; uncertain whether differences are statistically significant

Head-specific findings unexplained: Observation that heads are up-effective vs down-effective is interesting but lacks mechanistic understanding; speculation about functional roles (global retrieval vs structural parsing) is not rigorously supported

Limited generalization analysis: Evaluation only on instruction-tuned models (Llama-3.1-Instruct, Llama-2-Chat, Qwen-2); no evaluation on base models; unclear if improvements stem from instruction tuning or general LLM behavior; no architectural generalization beyond Transformers
Code availability incomplete: Abstract states code 'available a' (appears truncated); reproducibility package status unclear; hyperparameter selection process not fully transparent
